catalog_quote: As in Siamese, the syllable is an important unit in Lungchow phonology. It is bound by inter-syllabic junctures, represented by spaces in our orthography. The intrasyllabic juncture is not specially marked, except by the lack of space between letters. 1.5.8. Stress and intonation. The Lungchow dialect does not have a strong contrast between different stresses, and no specific study has been made of its stress patterns or of its intonation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lungchow (Longzhou) Zhuang is a six-tone language in which every syllable carries a tone; Li states that the dialect has no strong contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables, i.e. stress is not prominent and not distinctive, and that its stress patterns have not been studied. No position of word stress is given. (For the Po-ai dialect in the same book Li adds that final particles/enclitics are usually less stressed; that remark is not made for Lungchow.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Lungchow; Li explicitly says no specific study of its stress patterns exists.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement about the dialect as a whole (word- and phrase-level stress together with intonation); based on Li's field data from the city of Lungchow (Longzhou), the eponymous variety of Zuojiang Zhuang. Access via Google Books full-text snippets of a copyrighted print book: two overlapping snippets give the complete sentence, but the page number is not visible.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is about Li Fang-Kuei's 'Lungchow' = the dialect of Longzhou city (龙州), the eponymous and representative variety of Zuojiang Zhuang (ISO 2006-128 lists 'Longzhou' and 'Nung Chao' as alternate names of zzj; Chinese sources call it 壮语南部方言左江土语, Glottolog has no separate languoid for the Longzhou dialect). Gedney/Hudak's Lungming (Longming, Tiandeng county) is also inside the zzj area per the ISO request. Note Pittayaporn 2009 finds Zuojiang not to be a single clade, and the Chinese Wikipedia lists Leiping 土话, Jinlong 岱话 and Longzhou as distinct sub-varieties; Li Shenglan 2022 describes the Jinlong 岱话 lect, not Longzhou city.

sources.note: Nothing on any modern Zuojiang variety. Lungchow (LC, from Li 1977) is its Central Tai representative; Lungming, Ningming, Chongzuo, Fusui forms cited. 'Stress' appears only in the Proto-Tai sesquisyllable argument (unstressed minor + stressed major syllable) and in a remark that *mɯŋA/*maɰA were possibly unstressed pronoun forms.

sources.note: Silent. Syllable = initial + nucleus + optional final, each syllable carries tone; six tones on open syllables (55, 45, 33 glottalized, 21, 11, 212 glottalized), checked-syllable tones conditioned by vowel length, historical tone-box splits, consonant and vowel inventories, consonant assimilation of the enclitic article -a, rhyme chart. No occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the whole phonology section (a full-text search for stress/accent = 0). Lungming = Longming, Tiandeng county, inside the zzj area.
